title: A2 consolidation
objectives: I can hold a longer conversation about my life: meet someone new, say what I did, what I am doing and what I will do, and choose the aspect of each verb.
I can manage everyday errands at the post office, the pharmacy and the railway station.
I can ask about the language in Ukrainian: what a word means, how to say something, and that someone repeat or explain it more slowly.
I can choose the case of a noun in the singular and the plural, and give its ending from its gender and its stem.
I can tell location from direction, choose between the paired verbs of motion, and use 'до ре́чі', 'напри́клад', 'здає́ться', 'спра́вді' and 'взагалі́' to organize what I say.

vocabulary.note: 'Означа́ю', 'означа́єш', like 'чита́ти'. The word or the thing that has a meaning is the subject, and the meaning is the object: 'Це сло́во означа́є ча́шку.' In this sense the verb has no perfective partner.

example.target: Я не зна́ю, що означа́є це сло́во.
example.source: I don't know what this word means.
example.source_literal: I not know, what means this word.

vocabulary.note: 'Повторю́', 'повто́риш': the stress moves from the ending to the stem after the 'я' form. Imperfective partner 'повто́рювати' ('повто́рюю', 'повто́рюєш'). 'Повторі́ть, будь ла́ска.' asks someone you call 'ви' to say something again; to a friend you say 'Повтори́, будь ла́ска.'

'Поясню́', 'поя́сниш', with the stress moving as in 'повтори́ти'. Imperfective partner 'поя́снювати' ('поя́снюю', 'поя́снюєш'). The person who is told is in the dative and the thing explained in the accusative: 'поясни́ти Се́мові сло́во'.

example.target: Іри́на Петрі́вна поясни́ла нам нову́ те́му.
example.source: Iryna Petrivna explained the new topic to us.
example.source_literal: Iryna Petrivna explained to-us new topic.

vocabulary.note: 'Запита́ю', 'запита́єш', like 'чита́ти'. Imperfective partner 'пита́ти'. The person asked is in the accusative, and what you ask about follows 'про' with the accusative: 'запита́ти вчи́тельку про те́му'. It means to ask in order to learn something, not to ask for a thing.

example.source: I asked Oksana where the railway station was.

vocabulary.note: 'Відпові́м', 'відповіси́', 'відпові́сть', 'відповімо́', 'відповісте́', 'відповідя́ть', like 'да́ти'; past 'відпові́в', 'відпові́ла'. Imperfective partner 'відповіда́ти' ('відповіда́ю'). The person answered is in the dative, and the question follows 'на' with the accusative: 'відпові́сти вчи́тельці на пита́ння'.
A neuter noun in '-я' after a doubled consonant, like 'життя́'. Genitive 'пита́ння', plural 'пита́ння', genitive plural 'пита́нь'.
A feminine noun in a consonant, like 'сіль': genitive 'ві́дповіді', instrumental 'ві́дповіддю'. Plural 'ві́дповіді', genitive plural 'ві́дповідей'. It shares its root with 'відпові́сти'.

Genitive plural 'поми́лок', with an inserted 'о'. To make a mistake is 'зроби́ти поми́лку', and to make mistakes in general is 'роби́ти поми́лки': Ukrainian uses 'роби́ти', to do, where English says 'make'.

example.source: There are two mistakes in this sentence.

vocabulary.source: to get acquainted, to meet for the first time
vocabulary.note: 'Познайо́млюся', 'познайо́мишся', 'познайо́мляться': after 'м' the 'я' and 'вони́' forms add 'л', as in 'люблю́'. Imperfective partner 'знайо́митися'. The person you meet is in the instrumental after 'з': 'познайо́митися з Ма́ртою'. It has the root of 'знайо́мий', acquaintance.

example.target: Ми познайо́милися в Ки́єві рік тому́.
example.source: We met in Kyiv a year ago.
example.source_literal: We got-acquainted in Kyiv year ago.

vocabulary.note: A talk between two or more people. A conversation in Ukrainian is 'розмо́ва украї́нською'.

example.source: It was a very interesting conversation.

vocabulary.note: 'Це пра́вда.' means 'That's true.' Alone, as a question, 'Пра́вда?' means 'Really?'. At the end of a statement it asks the listener to agree, like English 'isn't it?': 'Ки́їв вели́кий, пра́вда?'
It introduces an example and stands apart from the rest of the sentence, between commas. It is built from 'на' and 'при́клад', an example.

example.target: Я люблю́ украї́нську ї́жу, напри́клад, борщ і варе́ники.
example.source: I love Ukrainian food, for example borscht and varenyky.

vocabulary.note: 'Ре́чі' is the genitive of 'річ', thing, after 'до'. The phrase brings in something that has just come to mind and is connected with what is being said. It stands apart, between commas.

example.target: До ре́чі, ти вже купи́в квито́к?
example.source: By the way, have you bought the ticket yet?
example.source_literal: To thing, you already bought ticket?

vocabulary.note: The 'він' form of the verb 'здава́тися', to seem, used as a parenthetical word: it comments on the whole sentence, stands between commas and shows that the speaker is not sure. 'Мені́ здає́ться, що...' (literally 'to-me it-seems that...') means 'I think that...'.
In a statement it confirms that something is so. Alone, as a question, 'Спра́вді?' means 'Really?', like 'Пра́вда?'.

example.source: The borscht really is very tasty.

vocabulary.note: When it sums something up, it means 'in general'. In a sentence with 'не' it means 'at all'.

example.source: Olena doesn't eat meat at all.

vocabulary.note: The subject of a conversation, a lesson or a text. 'Ціка́ва те́ма' is an interesting topic.

example.source: What is the topic of our conversation?

dialogues.title: Meeting Marta
dialogues.context: At Andrii's café Oksana introduces Sam to Marta, who has just moved to Kyiv from Kharkiv and studies at Oksana's university. Young people say 'ти' to each other from the first meeting. 'Знайо́мтеся', meet each other, is the imperative of 'знайо́митися', the imperfective partner of 'познайо́митися', and Oksana says it to both of them. The vocative of 'Ма́рта' is 'Ма́рто'.

lines.speaker: Окса́на
lines.target: Се́ме, Ма́рто, знайо́мтеся! Це Ма́рта, моя́ нова́ по́друга з університе́ту.
lines.source: Sam, Marta, meet each other! This is Marta, my new friend from university.
lines.source_literal: Sam, Marta, get-acquainted! This Marta, my new friend from university.

lines.speaker: Ма́рта
lines.target: Приві́т, Се́ме! Ду́же приє́мно познайо́митися.
lines.source: Hi, Sam! Very nice to meet you.
lines.source_literal: Hi, Sam! Very pleasant to-get-acquainted.

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Мені́ теж, Ма́рто. Окса́на вже бага́то про те́бе говори́ла.
lines.source: Nice to meet you too, Marta. Oksana has already told me a lot about you.
lines.source_literal: To-me too, Marta. Oksana already much about you talked.

lines.speaker: Ма́рта
lines.target: Пра́вда? А мені́ вона́ сказа́ла, що ти з Кана́ди й живе́ш у Ки́єві вже рік.
lines.source: Really? And she told me that you're from Canada and have been living in Kyiv for a year.
lines.source_literal: Truth? And to-me she said, that you from Canada and live in Kyiv already year.

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Так, спра́вді. Рік тому́ я взагалі́ не говори́в украї́нською.
lines.source: Yes, that's right. A year ago I didn't speak Ukrainian at all.
lines.source_literal: Yes, really. Year ago I at-all not spoke by-Ukrainian.

lines.speaker: Ма́рта
lines.target: А за́раз ти гово́риш ду́же до́бре!
lines.source: And now you speak very well!

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Дя́кую, але́ я ще роблю́ бага́то поми́лок. І ча́сто не розумі́ю, коли́ лю́ди гово́рять шви́дко.
lines.source: Thanks, but I still make a lot of mistakes. And I often don't understand when people speak fast.
lines.source_literal: I-thank, but I still make many of-mistakes. And often not understand, when people speak quickly.

lines.speaker: Ма́рта
lines.target: Се́ме, а що тобі́ найбі́льше сподо́балося в Ки́єві?
lines.source: Sam, what have you liked most in Kyiv?
lines.source_literal: Sam, and what to-you most pleased in Kyiv?

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Мені́ подо́бається все. Напри́клад, метро́ й ка́ва в Андрі́я. А найбі́льше мені́ сподо́балася зима́!
lines.source: I like everything. For example, the subway and the coffee at Andrii's. And most of all I liked the winter!
lines.source_literal: To-me pleases everything. For-example, subway and coffee at Andrii. And most to-me pleased winter!

lines.speaker: Ма́рта
lines.target: Зима́? Спра́вді? А мені́ здає́ться, що взи́мку тут ду́же хо́лодно.
lines.source: Winter? Really? I think it's very cold here in winter.
lines.source_literal: Winter? Really? And to-me it-seems, that in-winter here very cold.

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Так, хо́лодно, але́ в Кана́ді ще холодні́ше!
lines.source: Yes, it's cold, but in Canada it's even colder!
lines.source_literal: Yes, cold, but in Canada still colder!

lines.speaker: Окса́на
lines.target: До ре́чі, Ма́рто, що бу́де в п’я́тницю в бібліоте́ці?
lines.source: By the way, Marta, what's happening at the library on Friday?
lines.source_literal: To thing, Marta, what will-be on Friday in library?

lines.speaker: Ма́рта
lines.target: Ко́жну п’я́тницю ми там зустріча́ємося й гово́римо украї́нською. Цього́ ти́жня в нас те́ма «Зима́».
lines.source: Every Friday we meet there and speak Ukrainian. This week our topic is winter.
lines.source_literal: Each Friday we there meet and speak by-Ukrainian. Of-this of-week at us topic «Winter».

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: До́бре! Я обов’язко́во бу́ду.
lines.source: Great! I'll definitely be there.
lines.source_literal: Good! I definitely will-be.

dialogues.title: Words from Lviv
dialogues.context: After class Sam stays behind to ask Iryna Petrivna about words he heard on a weekend trip to Lviv. Teacher and student say 'ви' to each other. 'Дя́кувати' is the infinitive of 'дя́кую', and 'нема́ за що' is literally 'there-is-not for what'.

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Іри́но Петрі́вно, мо́жна вас запита́ти? У ме́не є кі́лька пита́нь.
lines.source: Iryna Petrivna, may I ask you something? I have a few questions.
lines.source_literal: Iryna Petrivna, possible you to-ask? At me is several of-questions.

lines.speaker: Іри́на Петрі́вна
lines.target: Звича́йно, Се́ме. Пита́йте.
lines.source: Of course, Sam. Go ahead and ask.
lines.source_literal: Ordinarily, Sam. Ask.

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: На вихідни́х я ї́здив до Льво́ва. У кафе́ офіціа́нтка сказа́ла: «Ось ва́ша філіжа́нка ка́ви». Що означа́є «філіжа́нка»?
lines.source: On the weekend I went to Lviv. In a café the waitress said, 'Here is your cup of coffee.' What does 'філіжа́нка' mean?
lines.source_literal: On weekend I went to Lviv. In café waitress said: «Here your філіжа́нка of-coffee». What means «філіжа́нка»?

lines.speaker: Іри́на Петрі́вна
lines.target: Це мала́ ча́шка для ка́ви. Так ча́сто ка́жуть у Льво́ві.
lines.source: It's a small cup for coffee. People in Lviv often say that.
lines.source_literal: This small cup for coffee. So often they-say in Lviv.

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: А в Ки́єві мене́ зрозумі́ють, якщо́ я так скажу́?
lines.source: And will people in Kyiv understand me if I say that?
lines.source_literal: And in Kyiv me they-will-understand, if I so will-say?

lines.speaker: Іри́на Петрі́вна
lines.target: Так, зрозумі́ють. Це украї́нське сло́во, і його́ зна́ють усі́.
lines.source: Yes, they will. It's a Ukrainian word, and everyone knows it.
lines.source_literal: Yes, they-will-understand. This Ukrainian word, and it know all.

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: А ще, коли́ я сказа́в «дя́кую», чолові́к на вокза́лі відпові́в: «Нема́ за що». Що це означа́є?
lines.source: Also, when I said 'thank you', a man at the railway station answered, 'Нема́ за що.' What does that mean?
lines.source_literal: And also, when I said «I-thank», man on railway-station answered: «There-is-not for what». What this means?

lines.speaker: Іри́на Петрі́вна
lines.target: Так ка́жуть, коли́ хтось дя́кує. Це означа́є, що дя́кувати не тре́ба.
lines.source: People say it when someone thanks them. It means that there is no need to thank them.
lines.source_literal: So they-say, when someone thanks. This means, that to-thank not necessary.

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Ви́бачте, я не зрозумі́в. Поясні́ть, будь ла́ска, ще раз, пові́льніше.
lines.source: Sorry, I didn't understand. Please explain once more, more slowly.
lines.source_literal: Excuse-me, I not understood. Explain, be kindness, more time, more-slowly.

lines.speaker: Іри́на Петрі́вна
lines.target: Ви ка́жете «дя́кую», а вам відповіда́ють «нема́ за що». Мо́жна тако́ж сказа́ти «будь ла́ска».
lines.source: You say 'thank you', and people answer 'you're welcome'. You can also say 'будь ла́ска'.
lines.source_literal: You say «I-thank», and to-you they-answer «there-is-not for what». Possible also to-say «be kindness».

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Розумі́ю! І ще одне́ пита́ння. Оди́н хло́пець сказа́в: «Я взагалі́ не п’ю ка́ву». Що тут означа́є «взагалі́»?
lines.source: I see! And one more question. A young man said, 'Я взагалі́ не п’ю ка́ву.' What does 'взагалі́' mean here?
lines.source_literal: I-understand! And more one question. One young-man said: «I at-all not drink coffee». What here means «взагалі́»?

lines.speaker: Іри́на Петрі́вна
lines.target: Тут це означа́є, що він ніко́ли не п’є ка́ву.
lines.source: Here it means that he never drinks coffee.
lines.source_literal: Here this means, that he never not drinks coffee.

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Дя́кую за ві́дповіді, Іри́но Петрі́вно! Ви ду́же до́бре поя́снюєте.
lines.source: Thank you for the answers, Iryna Petrivna! You explain things very well.
lines.source_literal: I-thank for answers, Iryna Petrivna! You very well explain.

lines.speaker: Іри́на Петрі́вна
lines.target: Нема́ за що, Се́ме!
lines.source: You're welcome, Sam!
lines.source_literal: There-is-not for what, Sam!

dialogues.title: A day of errands
dialogues.context: On Friday Sam has errands to run before a trip to Odesa. On his way to the railway station he gets a call from Oksana, and then he buys a ticket from Bohdan at the station. Sam and Oksana say 'ти' to each other; Sam and Bohdan say 'ви'. 'Відпра́вити' means 'to send', and 'Слу́хаю вас', literally 'I-listen you', is how a clerk asks what you need.

lines.speaker: Окса́на
lines.target: Приві́т, Се́ме! Де ти за́раз?
lines.source: Hi, Sam! Where are you now?

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Приві́т! Я йду на вокза́л. Я вже був на по́шті й відпра́вив ма́мі пода́рунок.
lines.source: Hi! I'm on my way to the railway station. I've already been to the post office and sent my mom a present.
lines.source_literal: Hi! I go on railway-station. I already was on post-office and sent to-mom present.

lines.speaker: Окса́на
lines.target: До́бре! А в апте́ку ти ходи́в?
lines.source: Good! And did you go to the pharmacy?
lines.source_literal: Good! And in pharmacy you went?

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Так, ходи́в. У ме́не ще тро́хи боли́ть го́рло, тому́ я купи́в лі́ки.
lines.source: Yes, I did. My throat still hurts a little, so I bought some medicine.
lines.source_literal: Yes, went. At me still a-little hurts throat, therefore I bought medicine.

lines.speaker: Окса́на
lines.target: А квито́к до Оде́си ти вже купи́в?
lines.source: And have you bought the ticket to Odesa yet?
lines.source_literal: And ticket to Odesa you already bought?

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Ще ні. Куплю́ че́рез п’ять хвили́н.
lines.source: Not yet. I'll buy it in five minutes.
lines.source_literal: Still no. I-will-buy through five of-minutes.

lines.speaker: Богда́н
lines.target: До́брий день! Слу́хаю вас.
lines.source: Good afternoon! How can I help you?
lines.source_literal: Good day! I-listen you.

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Мені́ тре́ба квито́к до Оде́си на неді́лю, будь ла́ска.
lines.source: I need a ticket to Odesa for Sunday, please.
lines.source_literal: To-me necessary ticket to Odesa on Sunday, be kindness.

lines.speaker: Богда́н
lines.target: Є мі́сце в купе́, у шо́стому ваго́ні. По́їзд о деся́тій ве́чора.
lines.source: There's a seat in a compartment, in car six. The train is at ten in the evening.
lines.source_literal: Is place in compartment, in sixth car. Train at tenth of-evening.

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Перепро́шую, ви гово́рите ду́же шви́дко. Повторі́ть, будь ла́ска, пові́льніше.
lines.source: I beg your pardon, you're speaking very fast. Please repeat that more slowly.
lines.source_literal: I-beg-pardon, you speak very quickly. Repeat, be kindness, more-slowly.

lines.speaker: Богда́н
lines.target: Звича́йно. Мі́сце в купе́. Ваго́н шо́стий. По́їзд о деся́тій ве́чора.
lines.source: Of course. A seat in a compartment. Car six. The train is at ten in the evening.
lines.source_literal: Ordinarily. Place in compartment. Car sixth. Train at tenth of-evening.

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Дя́кую. А що означа́є «купе́»?
lines.source: Thank you. And what does 'купе́' mean?
lines.source_literal: I-thank. And what means «купе́»?

lines.speaker: Богда́н
lines.target: Це мала́ кімна́та у ваго́ні. Там ви бу́дете спа́ти.
lines.source: It's a small room in the railway car. That's where you will sleep.
lines.source_literal: This small room in car. There you will to-sleep.

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: До́бре, я візьму́ цей квито́к.
lines.source: Good, I'll take this ticket.

grammar.title: Spelling and sound: пита́ння, ві́дповідь, до ре́чі and the other new words
grammar.explanation:
Every new word in this unit can be read with the rules of the alphabet units and the unit on stress, and none needs a new rule. Three of them show rules worth seeing again.

'Пита́ння' [pɪˈtɑnʲːɑ] has a doubled 'нн'. Two equal consonant letters are said as one long consonant, held a little longer than a short one, as in 'життя́', and here it is soft because 'я' follows it. Like 'життя́' and 'ре́чення', the word is a neuter noun in '-я' after a doubled consonant. In the genitive plural 'пита́нь' no vowel follows, only one 'н' is written, and the soft sign keeps it soft.

'Ві́дповідь' [ˈʋʲidpɔʋʲidʲ] has three syllables and is stressed on the first. Both letters 'в' are [ʋ], because a vowel follows each of them, and both are soft before 'і'. The first 'д' stands before the voiceless 'п' and stays voiced, as the 'д' of 'шви́дко' does before 'к'; among the voiced consonants only 'г' changes before a voiceless one, as in 'легки́й'. The last 'дь' is a soft [dʲ], and it too stays voiced at the end of the word, as the 'б' of 'хліб' does.

'До ре́чі' is two words. 'До' has one syllable and carries no mark. 'Ре́чі' is the genitive of 'річ', thing: the 'і' of 'річ' stands in a closed syllable, and when the ending '-і' opens the syllable it goes back to 'е', as 'кіт' gives 'кота́' and 'ніч' gives 'но́чі'. The 'р' is hard before 'е', and the 'ч' is hard, only slightly softened before 'і'.

The other new words apply familiar rules:

- 'Здає́ться' [zdɑˈjɛt͡sʲːɑ] has 'є' after the vowel 'а', so it is [j] plus [ɛ], and ends in '-ться', said as one long soft 'ц', as in 'прокида́ється'.
- 'Повтори́ти' [pɔwtɔˈrɪtɪ] has 'в' before 'т', said [w], as in 'жо́втий'. Its stress moves after the 'я' form: 'повторю́', but 'повто́риш'.
- 'Поясни́ти' [pɔjɑsˈnɪtɪ] has 'я' after the vowel 'о', so it is [j] plus [ɑ]. Its stress moves in the same way: 'поясню́', but 'поя́сниш'.
- 'Познайо́митися' has 'йо' after a vowel, said [jɔ], as in 'знайо́мий'. In 'познайо́млюся' an 'л' is inserted after 'м', as in 'люблю́'.
- 'Спра́вді' [ˈsprɑwdʲi] and 'пра́вда' [ˈprɑwdɑ] have 'в' before 'д', said [w]; in 'спра́вді' the 'д' is soft before 'і'.
- 'Взагалі́' [wzɑɦɑˈlʲi] begins with 'в' before a consonant, said [w], as in 'вдо́ма', and its 'г' is the voiced [ɦ].
- 'Поми́лка' has a hard 'л' before 'к'. Its genitive plural 'поми́лок' inserts an 'о' between them, as 'пля́шка' gives 'пля́шок'.
- 'Напри́клад' ends in a 'д' that stays voiced at the end of the word.

grammar.title: The seven cases: what each one does
grammar.explanation:
A Ukrainian noun has seven cases. A case is a set of endings that shows what job the noun does in the sentence, where English uses word order and prepositions. You have now met every case in the singular and in the plural, and two questions decide which one a noun takes.

The first question is whether a preposition stands before the noun. Every preposition takes a particular case, and a few take two cases with two meanings:

- 'у' and 'на' take the locative for where something is ('у мі́сті') and the accusative for where it goes ('у мі́сто')
- 'з' takes the genitive for 'from' ('з Ки́єва') and the instrumental for 'with' ('з дру́гом')
- 'за' takes the instrumental for 'behind' ('за до́мом') and the accusative for 'for' after 'дя́кувати' ('Дя́кую за пора́ду.')

If there is no preposition, the second question is what job the noun does. The subject is in the nominative, the direct object in the accusative, the person who receives or experiences something in the dative, the means or the role in the instrumental, and the owner or a quantity in the genitive.

Some words choose a case of their own, and it is learned with the word:

- the genitive after 'нема́є', after numbers from five up, and after 'бага́то', 'ма́ло', 'кі́лька' and 'до́сить'
- the dative with 'подо́батися', 'тре́ба', 'мо́жна', 'шко́да', 'допомага́ти', 'дзвони́ти' and 'ра́дити'
- the instrumental with 'займа́тися', 'цікави́тися' and 'ста́ти', and with 'працюва́ти' for a role

The vocative is not a job in the sentence but the form for calling someone: 'Ма́рто!', 'Се́ме!'.

An adjective, a possessive or a demonstrative before a noun takes the noun's case, gender and number: 'з мої́м ста́ршим бра́том', 'у вели́кому мі́сті', 'для на́ших дру́зів'. A pronoun has its own forms in every case: 'мене́', 'мені́', 'мно́ю', 'на мені́'.

grammar.title: Hard stems: the three genders in the singular and the plural
grammar.explanation:
A noun's endings depend on its gender and on its stem, the part that is left when the ending is taken off. A hard stem ends in a hard consonant: 'студе́нт-', 'мам-', 'міст-'. The table gives one model noun of each gender with a hard stem, and most of the nouns you know decline like one of them. The plural column gives the plural of all three.

In the singular, remember these points:

- Masculine and neuter nouns share the genitive '-а', the instrumental '-ом' and the locative '-і'. They differ in the nominative, in the accusative of people, and in the dative and the locative, where a masculine noun for a person prefers '-ові' ('студе́нтові', 'на студе́нтові').
- A masculine noun for a person or an animal uses its genitive form as its accusative ('Я ба́чу студе́нта.'); a thing keeps the nominative form ('Я ба́чу стіл.').
- Many masculine nouns for substances, places, institutions and abstract things take '-у' in the genitive ('су́пу', 'па́рку', 'ча́су'), and many with a stem in 'к', 'г' or 'х' take '-у' in the locative ('у па́рку', 'на ри́нку').
- Feminine nouns have the most varied endings, with a different one in almost every case: '-а', '-и', '-і', '-у', '-ою', '-і', '-о'.

In the plural the three genders almost merge. Every noun ends in '-ам' in the dative, '-ами' in the instrumental and '-ах' in the locative. Only two plural forms still depend on gender:

- the nominative: '-и' for most masculine and feminine nouns ('студе́нти', 'ма́ми'), and '-а' for neuter nouns ('міста́')
- the genitive: '-ів' for masculine nouns ('студе́нтів'), and no ending at all for feminine and neuter nouns ('мам', 'міст'), with an 'о' or 'е' inserted where two consonants would end the word ('пля́шок', 'ві́кон')

The accusative plural is the genitive form for people and animals ('Я ба́чу студе́нтів.') and the nominative form for things ('Я ба́чу міста́.'). The stress often moves in the plural ('мі́сто', 'міста́'; 'сестра́', 'се́стри'), so learn it with the plural form.

grammar.title: Soft stems, nouns in a consonant and the changes in the stem
grammar.explanation:
The second pattern is the soft one. It covers masculine nouns in '-ь' or '-й' and many in '-р' ('вчи́тель', 'музе́й', 'лі́кар'), feminine nouns in '-я' ('ву́лиця', 'ку́хня', 'неді́ля') and neuter nouns in '-е' ('мо́ре', 'се́рце'). The soft endings are the hard ones written with the vowel letter that keeps a consonant soft:

- 'я' for 'а' and 'ю' for 'у': 'мо́ря', 'мо́рю', 'ву́лицю'
- 'і' for 'и': 'вчителі́', 'ву́лиці'
- 'е' for 'о' in the instrumental: 'вчи́телем', 'ву́лицею', 'мо́рем'
- '-ям', '-ями', '-ях' for '-ам', '-ами', '-ах' in the plural: 'вчителя́м', 'ву́лицями', 'на моря́х'

Nouns whose stem ends in 'ж', 'ч', 'ш' or 'щ' are a mixed group. These consonants are hard, so the nouns write 'а' and 'у' where a soft stem writes 'я' and 'ю' ('пло́ща', 'пло́щу'), but they take the soft endings in 'і' and 'е' ('пло́щі', 'пло́щею', 'ключі́', 'ключе́м').

A third pattern belongs to feminine nouns that end in a consonant, such as 'сіль', 'ніч', 'о́сінь', 'по́дорож' and 'ві́дповідь'. The nominative and the accusative have no ending, the genitive, dative and locative end in '-і', and the instrumental ends in '-ю' with a single final consonant doubled: 'ві́дповіддю', 'сі́ллю', 'ні́ччю'. After 'б', 'п', 'в', 'м', 'ф' or 'р' the instrumental has an apostrophe instead ('ма́тір’ю'), and after two consonants nothing is doubled: 'ра́дість', joy, gives 'ра́дістю'. In the plural they take '-і', and '-ей' in the genitive ('ві́дповіді', 'ві́дповідей').

In every pattern the stem itself can change when an ending is added:

- An 'і' in the last, closed syllable goes back to 'о' or 'е' when an ending opens the syllable: 'стіл', 'стола́'; 'кіт', 'кота́'; 'річ', 'ре́чі'.
- An 'о' or 'е' before the last consonant drops out: 'ри́нок', 'на ри́нку'; 'ка́шель', 'ка́шлю'; 'квито́к', 'квитка́'.
- 'г', 'к' and 'х' become 'з', 'ц' and 'с' before the ending '-і': 'кни́га', 'у кни́зі'; 'апте́ка', 'в апте́ці'; 'по́друга', 'по́друзі'.
- An 'о' or 'е' is inserted in a genitive plural with no ending: 'поми́лка', 'поми́лок'; 'сестра́', 'сесте́р'; 'вікно́', 'ві́кон'.

grammar.title: Verbs: aspect, the tenses, the imperative and the conditional
grammar.explanation:
Every Ukrainian verb form answers two questions: when the action happens, and how the speaker presents it. The second question is aspect. An imperfective verb presents an action as a process, a habit or a plain fact; a perfective verb presents it as one completed whole with a result. Most verbs come in pairs ('роби́ти', 'зроби́ти'; 'купува́ти', 'купи́ти'; 'бра́ти', 'взя́ти'), so you choose the verb of the pair first and the tense second.

The two aspects have different sets of tenses:

- An imperfective verb has a past ('чита́в'), a present ('чита́ю') and two futures with the same meaning, the compound 'бу́ду чита́ти' and the one-word 'чита́тиму'.
- A perfective verb has a past ('прочита́в') and a future ('прочита́ю'), but no present: its forms with present endings are its future.

To choose the aspect, ask what matters to you:

- the result of one completed action: perfective ('Я вже купи́в квито́к.', 'Я куплю́ квито́к за́втра.')
- the process, its length or its repetition: imperfective ('Я ці́лий день писа́в.', 'Я ча́сто купу́ю тут ка́ву.')
- only the fact that the action happened: imperfective ('Ти чита́в цю кни́гу?' Have you read this book?)

The past agrees with the subject in gender and number, not in person: 'я чита́в' said by a man, 'я чита́ла' by a woman, 'ми чита́ли'. After 'якщо́' and 'коли́' an action still to come is in the future, where English uses the present: 'Якщо́ ти запита́єш, я відпові́м.' An action that began in the past and is still going on is in the present, often with 'вже', where English says 'have been': 'Я вже рік живу́ в Ки́єві.'

The imperative and the conditional are moods, and each can be formed from either aspect:

- The imperative is built on the stem of the present, or of the future of a perfective verb: 'чита́й', 'прочита́й', 'повтори́', 'поясні́ть'. A perfective imperative asks for one specific act ('Повторі́ть, будь ла́ска.'); an imperfective one invites, gives general advice or forbids ('Чита́йте ча́сто.', 'Не говорі́ть так шви́дко.').
- The conditional is the past form with 'би', or 'б' after a vowel, and serves for any time: 'Я б пої́хав до Оде́си.' (I would go to Odesa.)

grammar.title: Location and direction, and the verbs of motion
grammar.explanation:
English often asks 'where?' for both a place and a goal. Ukrainian keeps them apart: 'де?' asks where something is, 'куди́?' asks where it is going, and 'зві́дки?' asks where it comes from. Each question has its own construction:

- 'де?': 'у' or 'на' with the locative ('у мі́сті', 'на по́шті')
- 'куди́?': 'у' or 'на' with the accusative ('у мі́сто', 'на по́шту'), or 'до' with the genitive ('до Льво́ва', 'до ма́ми')
- 'зві́дки?': 'з' with the genitive ('з мі́ста', 'з по́шти')

A place keeps its preposition: a place that takes 'у' for location takes 'у' for direction, and a place that takes 'на' takes 'на' for both: 'у па́рку', 'у парк'; 'на по́шті', 'на по́шту'. 'До' is the usual choice for going to a person ('до лі́каря', 'до бабу́сі') and is common with cities, where 'у Львів' is correct as well. With a noun that never changes form, only the verb shows the difference: 'Я в кіно́.' (I'm at the movies) and 'Я йду в кіно́.' (I'm going to the movies).

The verbs of motion add a second choice. Each kind of movement has two imperfective verbs:

- 'іти́' and 'ї́хати' (on foot and by vehicle) describe one movement in one direction, now or on the way: 'Я йду на вокза́л.' (I'm on my way to the station.)
- 'ходи́ти' and 'ї́здити' describe movement in general: a habit, a trip there and back, an ability: 'Я ча́сто ї́жджу до Льво́ва.'

In the past, 'ходи́в' and 'ї́здив' say that someone went somewhere and came back: 'Учо́ра я ходи́в у кіно́.' The perfectives 'піти́' and 'пої́хати' say that someone set off: 'Він пої́хав до Оде́си.' (He has left for Odesa, and he is there or on the way.) Their future announces a trip: 'За́втра я пої́ду до Оде́си.' The same pairs exist for flying ('леті́ти', 'літа́ти'), carrying ('нести́', 'носи́ти'), transporting ('везти́', 'вози́ти') and running ('бі́гти', 'бі́гати').

grammar.title: Asking about the language
grammar.explanation:
When you do not understand something, the most useful thing is to say so in Ukrainian and keep the conversation in the language. Each of these requests is built from grammar you already know.

'Як сказа́ти украї́нською...?' is literally 'how to-say by-Ukrainian...?'. 'Сказа́ти' is the perfective infinitive of 'to say', and 'украї́нською' is the instrumental of the adjective 'украї́нська' in 'украї́нська мо́ва', with 'мо́вою' left out. The sentence has no subject: an infinitive after a question word asks what one should do, as in 'Що роби́ти?' (What should I do?). In speech you finish the question with the word you need in your own language, or you point at the thing: 'Як це сказа́ти украї́нською?' (How do you say this in Ukrainian?).

'Що означа́є це сло́во?' (What does this word mean?) has the word as its subject, and 'означа́є' agrees with it: literally 'what means this word?'. About something you can point at you ask 'Що це означа́є?', and the answer often begins 'Це означа́є, що...' (It means that...).

The requests to repeat, explain or write something are perfective imperatives, because each asks for one act. To someone you call 'ви' they end in '-іть' ('Повторі́ть', 'Поясні́ть', 'Напиші́ть'), and to a friend in '-и' ('Повтори́', 'Поясни́', 'Напиши́'). The request to speak more slowly uses the imperfective 'говори́ти', because it asks how someone should go on speaking: 'Говорі́ть, будь ла́ска, пові́льніше.' 'Пові́льніше' is the comparative of 'пові́льно', slowly, formed with '-іше' as 'нові́ший' is formed from 'нови́й'. 'Будь ла́ска' can stand at the start, in the middle or at the end, between commas.

'Ще раз' means 'once more'. It is 'ще', more, and 'раз', one time, a masculine noun.

To say that you did not understand, use the perfective 'зрозумі́ти', the partner of 'розумі́ти': 'Я не зрозумі́в.' said by a man, 'Я не зрозумі́ла.' said by a woman. It refers to one moment, what was just said, like English 'I didn't catch that'. 'Я не розумі́ю.' (I don't understand) uses the imperfective present and can also describe a general state.

grammar.title: Words that steer a conversation: до ре́чі, напри́клад, здає́ться, спра́вді, взагалі́
grammar.explanation:
Conversation needs words that add no new facts but show how the facts fit together: that a thought is an aside, an example, a guess or a confirmation. Several of them are parenthetical words. A parenthetical word comments on the whole sentence and is not part of its grammar: if you take it out, the sentence is still complete. In writing it stands between commas. In 'Здає́ться, Ма́рта вдо́ма.' (It seems Marta is at home.) the sentence 'Ма́рта вдо́ма.' is complete without 'здає́ться'.

The words of this unit work like this:

- 'До ре́чі' (by the way, literally 'to thing') brings in something that has just come to mind and is connected with the topic.
- 'Напри́клад' (for example) introduces one or more examples and stands between commas.
- 'Здає́ться' (it seems) is the 'він' form of 'здава́тися', to seem, used alone. It makes a statement less certain. With a person in the dative it gives an opinion: 'Мені́ здає́ться, що...' (I think that..., literally 'to-me it-seems that...'). The person is in the dative because the thing that seems is the subject, as with 'подо́батися'.
- 'Спра́вді' (really, indeed) confirms a statement and is not set off by commas: 'Це спра́вді до́бре.' Alone, with a rising voice, 'Спра́вді?' means 'Really?'.
- 'Пра́вда?' (literally 'truth?') also means 'Really?'. At the end of a statement it asks the listener to agree, like English 'isn't it?' or 'don't you?'.
- 'Взагалі́' means 'in general' when it sums something up, and then it stands between commas. In a sentence with 'не' it means 'at all' and is an ordinary adverb with no commas.

These words make speech sound natural, but one or two in a sentence are enough.

culture.title: Learning Ukrainian in Ukraine: speaking clubs and patient listeners
culture.text:
For a long time many Ukrainians, especially in the big cities, spoke Russian in daily life. Since Russia's full-scale invasion in February 2022, a great many of them have chosen to switch to Ukrainian at home, at work and online. A foreigner who learns Ukrainian in Kyiv is therefore not alone: adults of every age are learning the language or improving it too.

This has made the speaking club, 'розмо́вний клуб', a familiar part of city life. 'Розмо́вний' is the adjective of 'розмо́ва', conversation. A speaking club is a free meeting, often in a library, a café or a university, where people practice conversation. Each meeting has a topic, 'те́ма', and a host keeps the conversation going. Volunteer projects also run free online courses for adults.

Since 2021 the law has required shops, cafés, banks and other services to serve customers in Ukrainian, unless a customer asks for another language. In a shop or at a railway station in any city you will hear the forms this course teaches.

Most Ukrainians are glad to hear a foreigner speak their language and are patient with mistakes. A few habits help:

- Ask in Ukrainian, even when you know that the other person speaks English: 'Як це сказа́ти украї́нською?'
- Say plainly that you have not understood: 'Я не зрозумі́в' or 'Я не зрозумі́ла', then 'Повторі́ть, будь ла́ска, пові́льніше.'
- If someone switches to English to help you, it is polite to ask to go on in Ukrainian: 'Мо́жна украї́нською? Я вивча́ю мо́ву.' (Can we speak Ukrainian? I'm learning the language.)

People you meet will often pay you a compliment: 'Ви ду́же до́бре гово́рите украї́нською!' The polite reply is simply 'Дя́кую!'

It asks the listener to agree.
exercises.explanation: 'До ре́чі', literally 'to thing', means 'by the way'. An example is introduced by 'напри́клад', and 'пра́вда?' at the end of a statement asks for agreement.
The phrase is 'Ду́же приє́мно познайо́митися.', with the perfective infinitive of 'to get acquainted'.

exercises.hint_source: May I ask? I have a question.
exercises.explanation: 'Пита́ння' is a neuter noun with a doubled 'нн'. After 'у ме́не є' the thing owned is the subject, so it is in the nominative.

exercises.prompt: How is the doubled 'нн' in 'пита́ння' said?
choices: as two short consonants with a vowel between them
exercises.explanation: Two equal consonant letters are said as one long consonant, as in 'життя́', and the 'я' after them makes it soft.

exercises.prompt: Which case follows 'з' in 'Я познайо́мився з Ма́ртою.'?
exercises.explanation: 'З' meaning 'with' takes the instrumental: 'з Ма́ртою'. 'З' meaning 'from' takes the genitive: 'з Ки́єва'.

exercises.hint_source: I'm going to the post office.
exercises.explanation: Direction after 'на' takes the accusative: 'по́шта' becomes 'по́шту'. Location would be the locative, 'на по́шті'.
Location after 'у' or 'в' takes the locative '-і', and 'к' becomes 'ц' before it: 'апте́ка', 'в апте́ці'.

exercises.prompt: Sam goes to Lviv by train about once a month. How does he say 'I often go to Lviv'?
exercises.explanation: A habit, a trip made again and again, takes the verb of general motion 'ї́здити': 'ї́жджу'. 'Ї́ду' is one trip in one direction, and 'пої́ду' is one future departure.

exercises.hint_source: Yesterday Oksana went to the pharmacy on foot and came back.
exercises.explanation: A trip there and back in the past takes 'ходи́ти' on foot: 'ходи́ла' for a woman. The accusative 'в апте́ку' shows the direction.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence presents one completed action with a result?
exercises.explanation: The perfective 'прочита́в' presents the reading as finished. 'До́вго чита́в' presents a process, and 'ча́сто чита́ю' a habit.

exercises.hint_source: Have you already answered her question? (to a man)
exercises.explanation: One completed answer takes the perfective 'відпові́сти', and its past is 'відпові́в' for a man. The question answered follows 'на' with the accusative.

exercises.prompt_target: Чи не могли́ ___ ви поясни́ти це сло́во?
exercises.explanation: The polite request is 'Чи не могли́ б ви...?'. After the vowel of 'могли́' the particle is written 'б'.

exercises.hint_source: Please speak more slowly. (to a teacher)
exercises.explanation: To someone you call 'ви' the imperative of 'говори́ти' is 'говорі́ть'. The imperfective is used because the request is about how the person should go on speaking.

exercises.prompt: In 'Мені́ здає́ться, що Ма́рта вдо́ма.', why is 'мені́' in the dative?
choices: Because 'мені́' is the subject of the sentence.
Because the thing that seems is the subject, and the person to whom it seems is in the dative, as with 'подо́батися'.
exercises.explanation: 'Здає́ться' is a verb form, the 'він' form of 'здава́тися'. Its subject is what seems so, and the person is in the dative: literally 'to-me it-seems that Marta at-home'.
After 'п’ять' the noun is in the genitive plural. A feminine noun in '-а' has no ending there, and an 'о' is inserted between 'л' and 'к': 'поми́лок'.

exercises.hint_source: Iryna Petrivna explained the new topic to the students.
exercises.explanation: The people who are told something are in the dative, and the dative plural ends in '-ам' for every gender: 'студе́нтам'.

exercises.hint_source: My brother wants to become a doctor.
exercises.explanation: 'Ста́ти' takes the instrumental. 'Лі́кар' declines like a soft stem, so the instrumental is '-ем', as in 'вчи́телем'.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence says that Sam is at the post office?
exercises.explanation: Location after 'на' takes the locative: 'на по́шті'. 'На по́шту' is direction, and 'з по́шти' is where someone comes from.

exercises.prompt: Why is the 'д' doubled in 'ві́дповіддю', the instrumental of 'ві́дповідь'?
choices: Every instrumental doubles the last consonant of the stem.
The doubled letter marks the stressed syllable.
A feminine noun that ends in a single consonant doubles it before the instrumental ending '-ю'.
exercises.explanation: Feminine nouns in a single consonant take '-ю' in the instrumental and double the consonant before it: 'ві́дповіддю', like 'сі́ллю' and 'ні́ччю'. Other nouns do not: 'ма́мою', 'бра́том'.

exercises.prompt: In the first dialogue, why is Marta surprised that Sam likes the winter?
choices: She thinks that it is very cold in Kyiv in winter.
She thinks that Sam has never been in Kyiv in winter.
exercises.explanation: Marta says 'А мені́ здає́ться, що взи́мку тут ду́же хо́лодно.' Sam answers that in Canada it is even colder.

exercises.prompt: In the second dialogue, what does 'філіжа́нка' mean, according to Iryna Petrivna?
exercises.explanation: Iryna Petrivna says 'Це мала́ ча́шка для ка́ви.' and adds that people in Lviv often say it.

exercises.prompt: In the third dialogue, what has Sam not done yet when Oksana phones him?
choices: sent a present to his mom
exercises.explanation: Sam says 'Ще ні. Куплю́ че́рез п’ять хвили́н.' He has already been to the post office and to the pharmacy.

exercises.prompt: In the third dialogue, how does Bohdan explain the word 'купе́'?
choices: the sixth car of the train
a small room in the railway car where you sleep
exercises.explanation: Bohdan says 'Це мала́ кімна́та у ваго́ні. Там ви бу́дете спа́ти.'

exercises.audio_target: Ми вже рік живемо́ у Льво́ві.
choices: We lived in Lviv a year ago.
We have been living in Kyiv for a year.
We have been living in Lviv for a year.

exercises.audio_target: До ре́чі, ти вже купи́в квито́к до Оде́си?
choices: By the way, have you already bought the ticket to Odesa?
By the way, have you already bought the ticket to Lviv?
By the way, will you buy the ticket to Odesa?

exercises.prompt_source: If I had time, I would go to Odesa. (a man)
I didn't understand, please explain. (a man, to a teacher)
If you ask me, I'll answer. (to a friend)
Yesterday I went to the movies.

exercises.explanation: The word is the subject and 'означа́є' agrees with it. Ukrainian usually puts the subject after the verb in this question, but both orders are correct.

exercises.prompt_source: I have been living in Kyiv for a year.
answers: Я вже рік живу́ в Ки́єві.
Я живу́ в Ки́єві вже рік.
Уже́ рік я живу́ в Ки́єві.
Вже рік я живу́ в Ки́єві.
exercises.explanation: An action that began in the past and is still going on is in the present, often with 'вже': 'Я вже рік живу́ в Ки́єві.'
'Зроби́ти поми́лку' is one completed act, so the verb is perfective, and the past agrees with the speaker: 'зроби́в' for a man, 'зроби́ла' for a woman.

exercises.prompt_source: Please explain this word. (to a teacher)
exercises.explanation: To someone you call 'ви' the perfective imperative of 'поясни́ти' is 'поясні́ть'. The word explained is in the accusative, which for 'сло́во' is the same as the nominative.
One answer with a result is the perfective future 'відповімо́', formed like 'дамо́'. The imperfective futures of 'відповіда́ти' present the answering as a process.

exercises.hint_source: We have an interesting topic today.
